L127: **Dr. Markéta "Meg" Lawson (née Dvořáková)** (b. 1974, Brno, Czechoslovakia)
L128: - Nuclear engineer. PhD from MIT, Nuclear Science and Engineering, 2002. Dissertation: neutron transport modeling for mixed-oxide fuel assemblies. She can explain it in three sentences or three hours depending on who's asking.
L131: - Arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts in August 1996 with two suitcases and English she'd learned from textbooks and BBC World Service. Within a year, the accent was fading. Within five, Americans couldn't place it — something European, maybe German? — unless she was tired or angry, when the Czech consonants would surface like rebar through concrete. Twenty-eight years later, it comes out maybe twice a year. Embry has only heard it a handful of times. Each time, she knows her mother is furious.
L132: - Worked at Savannah River Site (2002–2010), then civilian nuclear consulting. She is the only Czech-born engineer most of her colleagues have ever met. She doesn't make it a topic. When people ask "where are you from?" she says "South Carolina." If they push — "originally?" — she says "Brno" and offers nothing else. Embry learned this deflection pattern before she knew where Brno was.
L133: - **Her hands** are "Sudoku hands" — clean, precise, never grease. She moisturizes. She does the NYT crossword in pen. Her Sudoku times are 12 seconds faster than Embry's best. Neither of them admits it's a competition. Both of them know.
L134: - Taught Embry Python at 14: "Engineers who can't code are engineers who can't check their own work." Used a Raspberry Pi. They built a temperature sensor together. It's still running in Loretta's garden, texting moisture readings to Meg's phone.
L135: - Taught Embry the Czech words for kitchen things without meaning to. *Nůž* (knife), *hrnec* (pot), *trouba* (oven). Embry's Czech is maybe thirty words, all domestic. She can't conjugate a single verb. She can order svíčková at a restaurant in Brno and pronounce it correctly. This is the extent of her bilingualism and she's embarrassed by it.
L136: - The voice Embry hears at 2am: *"You're not there to fit in. You're there to learn what you need. Then leave. Those people aren't your people. That's fine."* — This hits different knowing Meg said it from experience. She wasn't fitting in at MIT in 1996 either. She left anyway. With a PhD.
L137: - Lives in South Carolina now with Tommy. Consults remotely. Drives to Aiken for on-site work twice a month. Cooks svíčková on Sundays sometimes — beef sirloin in cream sauce with bread dumplings. Tommy eats it without complaint. Loretta tried it once, said "Well, that's interesting," and went back to her collards. There is a détente.
L138: - Makes bramboráky (Czech potato pancakes) when Embry visits. They're crispy, garlicky, and better than anything Embry can make in El Segundo. Embry has tried the recipe four times. It never turns out right. Meg says it's the potatoes. It's not the potatoes.
L139: - **How she shows love:** Clarity. She doesn't say "I love you" at the end of every call — she says it when she means it, which makes it land harder. She drove to Yale for the breakdown. She didn't hug Embry in the car. She bought her food, sat with her, and said "Now. Tell me what happened." That was better than a hug.
L140: - When Embry was very small, Meg sang Czech lullabies. *Halí belí* and *Spi, děťátko, spi*. Embry doesn't remember the words. She remembers the sound. Sometimes, falling asleep in El Segundo, she almost catches it.

*The academic line. Where the PhD comes from. Where the "check your own work" comes from. Where the green eyes come from. Less warm than the Lawsons, more precise — not cold, just Czech. The Dvořáks don't hug. They bring you food and sit with you until you eat it. Embry has her mom's brain and her dad's hands. The Dvořáks gave her one; the Lawsons gave her the other.*

### Grandparents

**Ing. Pavel Dvořák** (1942–2019)
- Nuclear engineer. Worked at ÚJV Řež (Nuclear Research Institute) outside Prague for 28 years, then consulting for the Dukovany nuclear power plant until retirement. Quiet, meticulous, kept a leather-bound notebook of handwritten equations. His handwriting was so precise it looked typeset — same in Czech as in English.
- Survived the normalization era. Never talked about it. When the Velvet Revolution came in 1989, he walked to Wenceslas Square, stood in the crowd, and walked home. That was his protest. Meg was 15 and wanted to join him. He said "Stay. Watch from the window." She has never forgiven this.
- Where mom got her brain. Where Embry got the Precision — the academic side of it — though she'd never frame it that way. She thinks the Precision is from dad's garage. It's from both.
- Died November 2019 — the year before the breakup with Kai. Pancreatic cancer, fast. Meg flew to Brno. Embry followed two days later. The funeral was in the cemetery at Židenice. It rained. Embry understood about half of what was said. She stood next to her mother and didn't let go of her arm.
- She has his slide rule in a box she hasn't unpacked. A Logarex, Czech-made, 1960s. He carried it through his entire career even after calculators. *"Důvěřuj nástroji, kterému rozumíš."* — Trust the tool you understand. Meg translated it for her once. Embry wrote it on a sticky note that's still on her desk somewhere.
- They weren't close the way she's close to Loretta. He wasn't warm. But he noticed her. Once, when she was 12, visiting Brno for summer, he watched her solve a puzzle cube and said — in careful English — "You think in systems. That is rare." She's never forgotten it.

**Milena Dvořáková (née Kratochvílová)** (b. 1945)
- Retired mathematics teacher. 36 years at Gymnázium Matyáše Lercha in Brno. Taught analysis and geometry to sixteen-year-olds who feared her. They should have.
- Lives in the apartment on Kounicova she and Pavel bought in 1972. Two rooms. Immaculate. Three framed photos of Embry in the hallway — one from the wedding, one from a summer visit at six, one from the Brno trip for Pavel's funeral.
- Calls Embry "miláčku" (darling) and "zlatíčko" (little gold one). Embry secretly loves both. She can't pronounce either correctly but tries.
- Still bakes koláče (fruit pastries) every Saturday. Sends care packages to South Carolina twice a year — koláče, Studentská čokoláda, and handwritten letters in Czech that Meg translates. Embry keeps the letters in the same drawer as the uncashed checks from — wait. Milena sends crowns, not checks. Small amounts in envelopes. Embry keeps them all.
- FaceTimes Embry every other Sunday through Meg's phone. Her English is functional but heavily accented. She asks if Embry is eating. She says "I love you, miláčku" before hanging up. It's always enough.
- Sharper than anyone gives her credit for. Taught mathematics for four decades. She can calculate a tip faster than Embry's phone. Once corrected Tommy's estimate on a garage project — in front of him — and was right. Tommy has never recovered.

### Mom

**Dr. Markéta "Meg" Lawson (née Dvořáková)** (b. 1974, Brno, Czechoslovakia)
- Nuclear engineer. PhD from MIT, Nuclear Science and Engineering, 2002. Dissertation: neutron transport modeling for mixed-oxide fuel assemblies. She can explain it in three sentences or three hours depending on who's asking.
- Grew up in Brno in the shadow of her father's work. Pavel was at Řež and then Dukovany — she understood reactor physics before she understood what the normalization period had cost her family. She knew she wanted out. Not out of Czech Republic. Out of the ceiling.
- Undergraduate at ČVUT Prague (Czech Technical University), nuclear engineering. Graduated top of her class, 1996. Applied to MIT because an American visiting professor told her she was wasting her time in Prague. She proved him wrong by getting in.
- Arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts in August 1996 with two suitcases and English she'd learned from textbooks and BBC World Service. Within a year, the accent was fading. Within five, Americans couldn't place it — something European, maybe German? — unless she was tired or angry, when the Czech consonants would surface like rebar through concrete. Twenty-eight years later, it comes out maybe twice a year. Embry has only heard it a handful of times. Each time, she knows her mother is furious.
